content.summary_of_the_paper: The papers proposes fully differentiable deep SDF model alignment as a faster alternative to ICP based refinement for 6d pose estimation from pointclouds. The experiments on multiple datasets and baselines show compare results to ICP with a 5-6x improvement in speed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
Simple idea and clear presentation

Weaknesses:
While the main argument for the new method is its improved speed over ICP, it is not mentioned which implemetation of ICP is used.
While the proposed fully differentiable SDF method is implemented on a GPU most ICP methods are implemented in CPU and the nearest neighbor search is usually the most expensive part. Without knowing about the implementation and parallelization of the baseline it is not possible to judge the improvements.
The alignment of poses using SDF is a quite common method (e.g. SDF2SDF), and it seems that the only novelty here is the use of a deep learned model that allows automatic differentiation.

It is also unclear how the proposed method behaves based on the initialization compare to ICP. An ablation on synthetic data with known initializations could help to find the strength and weaknesses of the proposed method.

Notes:
The reference for the LineMOD dataset (Wang et al., 2017) is not correct.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is easy to follow, but there are several grammar, spelling mistakes.
The value of the contribution remains unclear due to a lack of comparability and ablation.
The novelty of combining learned SDF shape models with SDF to pointcloud alignment is known in other settings.
The reproducibility seems okay.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Unfortunately the paper does not specify the details of the baseline method they compare against which makes it impossible to put evaluate the results of the comparison. It also does not provide ablations on the stability of the method compared to the baseline.
Therefore I would reject the paper in its current state.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new method for 6D pose refinement. In contrast to standard ICP, it proposes to 1) train a neural signed distance function (SDF) of the surface (obtained by point cloud), and 2) optimize the pose (minimize the distance estimated by the SDF from model vertices to the surface). The proposed method does not require supervision (GT poses and masks).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This is an interesting novel application of SDF, namely to 6D pose estimation. The experimental section shows empirically the superiority of the results.

The significance of the result is limited. The time required to refine the pose with SDF is shown to be lower than the time required for ICP, however in order to obtain the SDF itself one needs to train it for up to 10 minutes per scene, is this right? The competition, ICP, does not require such additional time. Moreover, for many applications scenes change often (e.g. robotics where robots change the scene constantly). In such applications, the suggested SDF approach is not practical. The claim of efficiency is not supported.

Table 2 was hard to read: it mixes a bunch of incomparable results (such as methods using different sensor input or supervision level). Could the authors organize it somewhat clearer?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity and quality is fair. In my opinion the paper approach is new. The results are probably reproducible.

The notation is somewhat loose. For example, it is not clear what happen with voxel index $i$ in (5). There is no definition of loss $\mathcal L$.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the outlook of the paper is positive, the results are interesting though are not very practical.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper describes an alternative algorithm of conventional ICP pose refinement. 
The key idea is to replace the online computation of point to plane distance with a much lightweight query operation, which queries against an implicit representation that was trained a priori. 
By pushing the point to SDF query score to zero via gradient descent, it is effectively functioning as a pose refining algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- One major claim of the proposed algorithm is "obvious advantage on running time", however it doesn't seem to report sufficient results and descriptions on this aspect. Specifically, the last 2 columns of Table 1 lists compute time, but without any details on which implementation / hardware they are comparing ICP and proposed algorithm with. Furthermore, the normal computation of ICP can also be batch pre-processed, which is in spirit similar to the fine-tuning step required by proposed method. A fair comparison would then require 1) counting pre-processing time of both methods, and 2) profile online part with similar recourse accessed.

- The pose refinement is done with first-order (e.g, pytorch adam). It could be interesting to evaluate with second order optimization (whether via unrolling or implicit differentiable), which could provide a better convergence.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The idea of applying implicit NN for iterative pose alignment is original to the best of my knowledge. 
The paper overall is easy to follow; there are a few typos here and there and a proof read could be helpful.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall the idea is quite interesting. 
However the current results seems a bit lacking to back up the claims: 1) performance wise the proposed method seems marginally improved over ICP baseline, which was a very classic algorithm with tons of refinement / variations available. It's a bit unclear whether we have applied a properly adapted ICP baseline here.  2) the time cost improvement claim is a bit fuzzy to tell given the lack of results and description (mentioned above as well). 
I would expect a more thorough experiment setup (without asking for new dataset!) to highlight the improvement of the proposed work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a method to refine the pose aligning the point cloud belonging to an object and the camera frame of reference by means of minimizing an SDF-based objective. The method requires training a neural network encoding the geometry of an object by learning the object’s SDF. The paper presents experiments on publicly available datasets such as LINEMOD, Occluded LINEMOD, and T-LOSS. These experiments show that the method performs roughly comparable to the baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. I think the idea of using an SDF as part of a point-cloud alignment problem is interesting.

Weaknesses:
1. Lack of clarity. The paper lacks important information to reproduce the results: 
- Overall, the paper lacks a clear high-level explanation of the proposed method. In particular, I think Fig. 2 is very hard to parse and fails to communicate the intuition or high-level idea of the proposed method. The section b) of Fig. 2 is quite convoluted and the text lacks details about how to parse the image. It is unclear to me how the features shown in Fig. 2 are extracted; what the positional embedding used is; and a justification of the architecture used for the “Surface Extractor” in the Figure. From the “Network Architecture” paragraph it seems like the proposed approach is just putting existing components together; this in my opinion decreases the novelty of the approach.
- What is the loss used in Eq. 7? I could not find any no discussion about it.
2. The estimation refinement process presented in Sec. 3.2 lacks details:
- The update step shown in Eq. 9 does not preserve the properties of a rotation matrix. It is unclear from Eq. 8 how the optimization problem ensures that the rotation estimates still belong to the SO(3) group. This is a crucial aspect since the paper states that it aims at refining a pose, and the formulation does not seem to be that solid.
- The method lacks robustness. This is because the formulation assumes that the pre-trained SDF function is perfect. However, this may not be the case and the estimates can be severely affected.
- The proposed method requires a pre-trained SDF function for every object. I think this is not scalable as it requires training several networks, increasing time and computational resources.
3. Insufficient experiments:
- The paper mainly claims that the proposed method is faster than ICP in the abstract and Table 1. Unfortunately, I don’t see a more complete experiment backing this up besides Table 1. In principle, comparing both methods is not a fair comparison because the proposed method uses GPUs and requires an SDF network for each object. Thus, the training time of each SDF network for each object is discounted in Table 1.
- The ablation study is quite limited. It is unclear an optimal number of iterations (or the value of n in Algo. 1). Second, there are other parameters that can affect the performance (e.g., L and L_max) of the proposed approach.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As stated above, I think using an SDF-based network as part of an alignment problem is interesting. However, I also think the formulation lacks robustness and may require a significant amount of work when a user is interested in a large number of objects. Also, the results show that the approach is pretty much comparable with the baselines and the benefit is not that clear. Lastly, the narrative of the paper needs improvement to make it easy for a reader to parse the figures and hence reproduce the method more easily.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although I think using an SDF-based network as part of an alignment problem is interesting, the practical benefit seems to be just only the gain in time. However, the proposed method requires an off-line stage where it needs to train SDF networks for every object, which also takes time. Thus, I am not convinced that the proposed method has a real practical benefit.

content.title: Fast 6D Object Pose Refinement via Implicit Surface Representation Driven Optimization
content.TL;DR: In this paper, we propose a simple yet efficient self-supervised point cloud aligenment method via implicit neural network, which can serve as an alternative of ICP to achieve fast and accurate pose refinement.
content.abstract:
Pose refinement after the initial pose estimator has been demonstrated to be effective for 6D object pose estimation. The iterative closest point (ICP) is the most popular refinement strategy, which however suffers from slow convergence due to the nature of iterative nonlinear optimization. In this paper, we propose a simple yet efficient self-supervised point cloud aligenment method via implicit neural network, which can serve as an alternative of ICP to achieve fast and accurate pose refinement. Our key idea is to encode the surface of target point cloud into a signed distance function (SDF); the optimal rigid transformation then can be derived by addressing a minimization problem over the SDF.  The workflow of our method does not require any pose annotations. Experimental results show our method can achieve 6.4\%, 16.2\%, and 3.9\% performance improvement over the prior art OVE6D (w/o ICP) on  LINEMOD, Occluded LINEMOD and T-LESS datasets respectively, and is comparable with other SOTA methods even the supervised ones.  Compared with point-to-plane ICP, our method has the obvious advantage on computation speed, due to the merit of full play to 
the high parallel characteristics of deep learning based on GPU acceleration.
